name: Science
description: Put on your explorer hat and discover how the world works! In this course you'll meet amazing plants and watch seeds burst into life, travel to forests and oceans to meet animals in their habitats, chase clouds and rain through the water cycle, and see how solids, liquids, and gases transform right before your eyes. Every topic is full of "wow" moments—why plants need sunlight, how animals find their homes, and what really happens when you mix things together!
You'll think like a real scientist: asking questions, making observations, and connecting the dots between nature and your everyday life. Get ready to look at the world in a whole new way!

lessons.title: Parts of a Plant
lessons.description: Learn about roots, stems, leaves, and flowers.

pages.title: Welcome to Parts of a Plant

sections.heading: What You'll Learn
body: In this lesson, you will learn about the four main parts of a plant: roots, stems, leaves, and flowers. Each part has a special job that helps the plant stay alive and grow. By the end, you'll be able to name each part and explain what it does!

sections.heading: What Do Roots Do?
body: Roots grow underground where you usually can't see them. Their job is to soak up water and nutrients from the soil, kind of like drinking through a straw. Roots also hold the plant in place so it doesn't fall over or blow away in the wind.

sections.heading: What Do Stems Do?
body: The stem is like a highway for the plant. It carries water and nutrients from the roots up to the leaves and flowers. Stems also hold the plant up tall so the leaves can reach the sunlight they need.

sections.heading: Why Are Leaves Important?
body: Leaves are the part of the plant that makes food. They use sunlight, water, and air to create energy the plant needs to grow. Most leaves are green because of a special substance called chlorophyll that helps capture sunlight.

sections.heading: What Do Flowers Do?
body: Flowers are not just pretty — they have a very important job! Flowers help the plant make seeds so new plants can grow. Bees and butterflies visit flowers and help spread pollen from one flower to another.

sections.heading: Remember the Four Parts
body: Every plant has roots, a stem, leaves, and flowers. Roots drink water, the stem carries it up, leaves make food from sunlight, and flowers help make seeds. Together, these parts keep the plant alive and growing!

question.text: Which part of a plant soaks up water from the soil?

lessons.title: What Plants Need
lessons.description: Discover that plants need sunlight, water, air, and soil.

video.title: Kurzgesagt – What Plants Need to Survive

sections.heading: What You'll Learn
body: In this lesson, you will discover the four things every plant needs to survive: sunlight, water, air, and soil. Without even one of these, a plant can get sick or die. By the end, you'll know exactly how to help a plant stay healthy!

sections.heading: Why Plants Need Sunlight
body: Plants need sunlight to make their own food through a process called photosynthesis. Without sunlight, a plant's leaves turn yellow and it stops growing. That's why you often see plants leaning toward a window — they're reaching for the light!

sections.heading: Why Plants Need Water
body: Water is like a plant's favorite drink. Roots pull water up from the soil and send it to every part of the plant. Water helps the plant stay stiff and strong, and without enough water, a plant will droop and wilt.

sections.heading: Why Plants Need Air
body: Plants breathe in a gas from the air called carbon dioxide. They use carbon dioxide along with sunlight and water to make food. Plants also release oxygen into the air, which is the gas that humans and animals need to breathe!

sections.heading: Why Plants Need Soil
body: Soil gives plants a place to stand and grow their roots. It also contains important nutrients — like vitamins for plants — that help them stay healthy and strong. Different plants like different types of soil, just like people like different foods.

sections.heading: The Four Things Plants Need
body: Remember, every plant needs sunlight, water, air, and soil. Sunlight gives energy, water keeps the plant hydrated, air provides carbon dioxide, and soil supplies nutrients. If you take care of all four, your plant will be happy and healthy!

question.text: Which gas do plants take in from the air to make food?

lessons.title: Seeds and Germination
lessons.description: Watch how a tiny seed sprouts into a plant.

sections.heading: What You'll Learn
body: In this lesson, you will learn what is inside a seed and how it sprouts into a new plant. This sprouting process is called germination. By the end, you'll understand the amazing journey a tiny seed takes to become a full-grown plant!

sections.heading: What's Inside?
body: A seed may be tiny, but it has everything it needs to grow a new plant. Inside, there is a baby plant called an embryo, plus stored food to help it start growing. The hard outer shell, called the seed coat, protects everything inside like a little suit of armor.

sections.heading: How Seeds Travel
body: Seeds have clever ways of getting to new places where they can grow. Some seeds blow in the wind like tiny parachutes. Others hitch a ride on animals' fur, float on water, or get carried inside fruits that animals eat.

sections.heading: What Is Germination?
body: Germination is when a seed starts to sprout and grow. First, the seed soaks up water and swells. Then a tiny root pushes out and grows down into the soil, and a little shoot grows up toward the sunlight.

sections.heading: What Seeds Need to Sprout
body: For germination to happen, a seed needs water, warmth, and air. The water softens the seed coat so the baby plant can break through. Warmth tells the seed that it's the right time to start growing, just like spring weather wakes up sleeping plants.

sections.heading: From Seed to Plant
body: Remember, a seed holds a tiny baby plant, stored food, and a protective coat. When it gets water, warmth, and air, it germinates — the root grows down and the shoot grows up. That's how every big tree and beautiful flower got its start!

question.text: What is it called when a seed starts to sprout and grow?

lessons.title: Photosynthesis for Kids
lessons.description: Learn how plants make their own food using sunlight.

sections.heading: What You'll Learn
body: In this lesson, you will learn how plants make their own food using sunlight, water, and air. This amazing process is called photosynthesis. By the end, you'll understand why plants are green and why they are so important for life on Earth!

sections.heading: The Recipe for Plant Food
body: Photosynthesis is like a recipe. Plants mix three ingredients: sunlight, water, and carbon dioxide from the air. The leaves act like tiny kitchens where these ingredients are combined to make sugar, which is the plant's food.

sections.heading: Why Are Leaves Green?
body: Leaves are green because they contain chlorophyll, a special substance that captures sunlight. Chlorophyll is what makes photosynthesis possible. It soaks up red and blue light from the sun and reflects green light back to our eyes — that's why we see green!

sections.heading: Oxygen for Us
body: During photosynthesis, plants release oxygen into the air as a bonus. This is the same oxygen that people and animals need to breathe! Without plants making oxygen, there wouldn't be enough clean air for us to survive.

sections.heading: Plants Feed the World
body: Almost all food on Earth can be traced back to photosynthesis. Plants use the sun's energy to make food, animals eat the plants, and then other animals eat those animals. Plants are at the very beginning of almost every food chain!

sections.heading: Photosynthesis Review
body: Photosynthesis is how plants make food from sunlight, water, and carbon dioxide. Chlorophyll in the leaves captures sunlight and turns these ingredients into sugar and oxygen. This process keeps plants alive and gives us the air we breathe!

question.text: What gas do plants release during photosynthesis?

lessons.title: Animal Groups
lessons.description: Meet mammals, birds, reptiles, fish, and amphibians.

sections.heading: What You'll Learn
body: In this lesson, you will meet five main groups of animals: mammals, birds, reptiles, fish, and amphibians. Scientists put animals into groups based on things they have in common. By the end, you'll be able to tell which group an animal belongs to!

sections.heading: What Are Mammals?
body: Mammals are warm-blooded animals that have hair or fur on their bodies. Mother mammals feed their babies milk. Dogs, cats, whales, and even humans are all mammals! Most mammals give birth to live babies instead of laying eggs.

sections.heading: What Are Birds?
body: Birds are warm-blooded animals that have feathers and wings. Most birds can fly, but some, like penguins and ostriches, cannot. All birds lay eggs with hard shells, and they have beaks instead of teeth.

sections.heading: Reptiles and Fish
body: Reptiles are cold-blooded animals with dry, scaly skin. Snakes, lizards, and turtles are all reptiles. Fish are also cold-blooded but they live in water and breathe through gills. Fish have fins and scales that help them swim.

sections.heading: What Are Amphibians?
body: Amphibians are special because they can live both in water and on land. Frogs, toads, and salamanders are amphibians. They start their lives in water breathing through gills, and as they grow up, they develop lungs to breathe air on land.

sections.heading: Five Animal Groups
body: Remember the five groups: mammals have fur and feed babies milk, birds have feathers, reptiles have scales, fish live in water with gills, and amphibians live in both water and on land. Knowing these groups helps you understand the animal kingdom!

question.text: Which animal group has feathers and lays eggs with hard shells?

lessons.title: What Is a Habitat?
lessons.description: Learn that a habitat is the place where an animal lives.

pages.title: Welcome to What Is a Habitat?

sections.heading: What You'll Learn
body: In this lesson, you will learn what a habitat is and why it matters for animals. A habitat is the natural home where an animal finds everything it needs to survive. By the end, you'll understand what makes a habitat just right for the animals that live there!

sections.heading: A Place to Call Home
body: A habitat is more than just a place — it's a home that gives an animal food, water, shelter, and space. A fish's habitat is the water in a pond, lake, or ocean. A bird's habitat might be a forest full of trees where it can build a nest.

sections.heading: Different Habitats for Different Animals
body: Every animal needs a habitat that fits its needs. A polar bear lives in the icy Arctic because it has thick fur to stay warm. A cactus wren lives in the hot desert because it can find water in cactus plants. Animals are adapted to their habitats!

sections.heading: Types of Habitats
body: There are many types of habitats on Earth. Forests, deserts, oceans, grasslands, and wetlands are just a few. Each habitat has its own climate, plants, and animals. Even a small pond in your backyard is a habitat for frogs and insects!

sections.heading: Why Habitats Need Protection
body: When a habitat is damaged or destroyed, the animals that live there can lose their homes. Pollution, cutting down trees, and building on wild land can hurt habitats. That's why it's important for people to protect natural places.

sections.heading: Habitats Are Important
body: A habitat provides food, water, shelter, and space for animals. Different animals need different habitats, and each animal is specially adapted to its home. Protecting habitats helps keep animals safe and healthy.

question.text: What four things does a habitat provide for an animal?

lessons.title: Forest Habitats
lessons.description: Explore the animals that live among the trees.

sections.heading: What You'll Learn
body: In this lesson, you will explore the forest habitat and meet some of the animals that live there. Forests are full of trees, plants, and wildlife. By the end, you'll understand how forest animals find food, shelter, and everything they need among the trees!

sections.heading: The Forest Floor
body: The forest floor is the ground layer covered with fallen leaves, moss, and tiny plants. Insects, worms, and mushrooms live here and help break down dead leaves into rich soil. Larger animals like foxes and rabbits also make their homes in burrows on the forest floor.

sections.heading: Animals That Dig and Hide
body: Many forest animals survive by digging or hiding. Rabbits dig burrows underground to stay safe from predators. Hedgehogs curl up in piles of leaves, and snakes hide under logs. The forest floor gives these animals plenty of places to stay hidden.

sections.heading: The Canopy Layer
body: High above the forest floor, the treetops form a leafy roof called the canopy. Birds build nests in the branches, and squirrels leap from tree to tree gathering nuts. The canopy gets lots of sunlight, which helps the leaves make food for the trees.

sections.heading: Forest Food Chains
body: In a forest, every living thing is connected through food chains. Trees and plants make food from sunlight, insects eat the plants, birds eat the insects, and hawks eat the birds. Each animal depends on others to survive, creating a web of life.

sections.heading: Forest Habitat Review
body: Forests have layers from the floor to the canopy, and each layer is home to different animals. Animals find food, shelter, and safety among the trees and plants. Everything in the forest is connected through food chains.

question.text: What is the leafy roof at the top of a forest called?

lessons.title: Ocean Habitats
lessons.description: Dive into the sea and meet ocean creatures.

sections.heading: What You'll Learn
body: In this lesson, you will dive into the ocean habitat and discover the amazing creatures that live there. The ocean covers most of our planet and is full of life. By the end, you'll know about different ocean zones and the animals that call the sea home!

sections.heading: Life Near the Surface
body: The sunlit zone is the top layer of the ocean where sunlight reaches. This is where you find sea turtles, dolphins, and jellyfish swimming around. Tiny plants called phytoplankton float here and make food using sunlight, just like plants on land.

sections.heading: Coral Reefs
body: Coral reefs are found in warm, shallow waters and are sometimes called the rainforests of the sea. They are built by tiny animals called coral polyps and are home to colorful fish, seahorses, and starfish. Coral reefs are bursting with life!

sections.heading: The Dark Zone
body: Deep below the surface, sunlight cannot reach and the water is very cold and dark. Strange creatures live here, like the anglerfish that has a glowing light on its head to attract prey. Giant squid and deep-sea jellyfish also call this dark world home.

sections.heading: Why the Ocean Matters
body: The ocean is incredibly important for life on Earth. It produces more than half of the oxygen we breathe and helps control our weather. Millions of animals depend on the ocean, and so do people who eat fish and seafood. Protecting the ocean protects us all!

sections.heading: Ocean Habitat Review
body: The ocean has different zones from the sunny surface to the dark deep sea. Each zone has its own special animals adapted to live there. The ocean produces oxygen, provides food, and is home to millions of creatures.

question.text: What are coral reefs sometimes called?

lessons.title: Types of Weather
lessons.description: Sunny, rainy, snowy, windy — learn them all.

sections.heading: What You'll Learn
body: In this lesson, you will learn about different types of weather including sunny, rainy, snowy, and windy days. Weather is what the sky and air are doing outside right now. By the end, you'll be able to describe the weather like a real meteorologist!

sections.heading: Sunny Days
body: On a sunny day, the sky is clear and the sun shines brightly. Sunny weather happens when there are few or no clouds blocking the sunlight. The sun warms the ground and the air, making it a great day to play outside!

sections.heading: Rainy Days
body: Rain falls when water droplets in clouds get too heavy and drop down to the ground. Rainy weather can be a gentle drizzle or a heavy downpour with thunder and lightning. Rain is very important because it gives water to plants, animals, and people.

sections.heading: Snowy Days
body: Snow happens when the air is cold enough for water in the clouds to freeze into ice crystals. These crystals stick together and fall as snowflakes. Every snowflake has a unique shape, and no two are exactly alike! Snow can cover the ground like a white blanket.

sections.heading: Windy Days
body: Wind is moving air that you can feel but cannot see. Wind happens because the sun heats the ground unevenly — warm air rises and cooler air rushes in to take its place. A gentle wind is called a breeze, while a very strong wind can be part of a storm.

sections.heading: Weather Review
body: Weather includes sunshine, rain, snow, and wind. Each type of weather is caused by the sun, air, and water working together. Learning about weather helps you decide what to wear and plan your day!

options: The moon pulling on the air
The sun heating the ground unevenly
question.answer: The sun heating the ground unevenly

lessons.title: The Water Cycle
lessons.description: Follow water as it moves from clouds to ground and back.

sections.heading: What You'll Learn
body: In this lesson, you will follow water on its amazing journey through the water cycle. Water moves from the ground to the sky and back again in a never-ending loop. By the end, you'll understand evaporation, condensation, and precipitation!

sections.heading: What Is Evaporation?
body: Evaporation is when the sun heats up water in rivers, lakes, and oceans, turning it into an invisible gas called water vapor. The water vapor floats up into the sky. You can see evaporation in action when a puddle disappears on a sunny day!

sections.heading: What Is Condensation?
body: When water vapor rises high into the sky, the air gets cooler. The cold air turns the water vapor back into tiny water droplets, and these droplets come together to form clouds. This is called condensation. It's like how a cold glass of water gets foggy on the outside.

sections.heading: What Is Precipitation?
body: When the tiny water droplets in clouds join together and get too heavy, they fall back down to Earth. This is called precipitation. Precipitation can be rain, snow, sleet, or hail depending on the temperature of the air.

sections.heading: Collection and Starting Over
body: After precipitation, water collects in rivers, lakes, oceans, and even underground. From there, the sun heats the water again and the whole cycle starts over. The water cycle has been going on for billions of years and never stops!

sections.heading: Water Cycle Review
body: The water cycle has four main steps: evaporation turns water into vapor, condensation forms clouds, precipitation brings water back to Earth, and collection gathers it in bodies of water. Then it all starts again!

question.text: What is it called when water vapor turns back into tiny water droplets in the sky?

lessons.title: Clouds and Rain
lessons.description: Find out what clouds are made of and why it rains.

sections.heading: What You'll Learn
body: In this lesson, you will discover what clouds are made of and learn about different types of clouds. You'll also find out why rain falls from the sky. By the end, you'll be able to look up and know what kind of cloud you see!

sections.heading: Clouds Are Made of Water
body: Clouds may look fluffy and soft, but they are actually made of billions of tiny water droplets or ice crystals floating in the air. These droplets are so light that they stay up in the sky. When enough droplets group together, we can see them as a cloud.

sections.heading: Types of Clouds
body: There are three main types of clouds. Cumulus clouds are big, white, and puffy like cotton balls and usually mean nice weather. Stratus clouds are flat and gray and can cover the whole sky. Cirrus clouds are thin and wispy, found very high up where it's cold.

sections.heading: How Rain Forms
body: Inside a cloud, tiny water droplets bump into each other and stick together to form bigger drops. When the drops get heavy enough, gravity pulls them down to the ground as rain. A single raindrop is made of about one million tiny cloud droplets!

sections.heading: Storm Clouds
body: Some clouds grow very tall and dark — these are called cumulonimbus clouds, or storm clouds. They can bring heavy rain, thunder, and lightning. You can often tell a storm is coming when you see dark, towering clouds building up in the sky.

sections.heading: Clouds and Rain Review
body: Clouds are made of tiny water droplets or ice crystals. There are different types of clouds like cumulus, stratus, and cirrus. Rain happens when water droplets in clouds get too heavy and fall to the ground.

question.text: Which type of cloud is big, white, and puffy like a cotton ball?

lessons.title: The Four Seasons
lessons.description: Explore spring, summer, fall, and winter.

sections.heading: What You'll Learn
body: In this lesson, you will explore the four seasons: spring, summer, fall, and winter. You'll learn what makes each season special and why seasons change throughout the year. By the end, you'll know what causes the seasons and what to expect in each one!

sections.heading: Spring — A Time for New Growth
body: Spring is when the world wakes up after winter. The weather gets warmer, flowers bloom, and trees grow new leaves. Baby animals are born, and birds return from their winter travels. Days start getting longer, which means more time to play outside!

sections.heading: Summer — The Warmest Season
body: Summer brings the longest days and the warmest weather. Plants are fully grown and fruits ripen on trees. Many animals are busy raising their young during summer. It's a great time for swimming, picnics, and enjoying the outdoors!

sections.heading: Fall — A Time for Change
body: In fall, the weather cools down and leaves change to beautiful colors like red, orange, and yellow before falling off the trees. Animals start preparing for winter by gathering food or growing thicker fur. The days get shorter and nights get longer.

sections.heading: Winter — The Coldest Season
body: Winter brings the coldest weather and the shortest days. In many places, snow covers the ground and lakes can freeze. Some animals hibernate, which means they go into a deep sleep to save energy. Other animals migrate to warmer places until spring returns.

sections.heading: Seasons Review
body: The four seasons — spring, summer, fall, and winter — happen because Earth is tilted as it moves around the sun. Each season brings different weather, and plants and animals change their behavior to match. The cycle repeats every year!

question.text: What do some animals do during winter to save energy?

lessons.title: Solids, Liquids, and Gases
lessons.description: Learn the three states of matter with everyday examples.

pages.title: Welcome to Solids, Liquids, and Gases

sections.heading: What You'll Learn
body: In this lesson, you will learn about the three states of matter: solids, liquids, and gases. Everything around you is made of matter, and it comes in one of these three forms. By the end, you'll be able to look around and identify solids, liquids, and gases everywhere!

sections.heading: What Is a Solid?
body: A solid has a definite shape and stays that way unless something changes it. Your desk, a rock, and an ice cube are all solids. The tiny particles inside a solid are packed tightly together, which is why solids don't change shape on their own.

sections.heading: What Is a Liquid?
body: A liquid can flow and takes the shape of whatever container it's in. Water, milk, and juice are all liquids. If you pour water from a cup into a bowl, the water changes shape to fill the bowl. The particles in a liquid move around more freely than in a solid.

sections.heading: What Is a Gas?
body: A gas spreads out to fill any space it's in. You can't usually see a gas, but it's all around you! The air you breathe is made of gases. The particles in a gas move very fast and are spread far apart, which is why gas doesn't have a fixed shape.

sections.heading: Matter Can Change States
body: Matter can change from one state to another. When you heat ice, it melts into water. When you heat water, it turns into steam, which is a gas. When you cool steam, it turns back into water. Temperature is what makes matter change states!

sections.heading: States of Matter Review
body: Solids keep their shape, liquids take the shape of their container, and gases spread out to fill any space. Heating and cooling can change matter from one state to another. Everything you see, touch, or breathe is made of matter!

question.text: What happens when you heat ice?

lessons.title: Properties of Matter
lessons.description: Describe objects by color, size, shape, and texture.

sections.heading: What You'll Learn
body: In this lesson, you will learn how to describe objects by their properties like color, size, shape, and texture. Properties are the special features that make each object unique. By the end, you'll be a pro at describing and comparing objects around you!

sections.heading: Describing by Color and Size
body: Color is one of the easiest properties to spot. A fire truck is red, a banana is yellow, and the sky is blue. Size tells you how big or small something is. You can compare objects by saying one is bigger, smaller, taller, or shorter than another.

sections.heading: Describing by Shape
body: Objects come in many different shapes. A ball is round, a book is rectangular, and a pizza slice is shaped like a triangle. Shape is an important property because it helps us tell objects apart and understand how they can be used.

sections.heading: What Is Texture?
body: Texture is how something feels when you touch it. A kitten's fur is soft, sandpaper is rough, a marble is smooth, and a pinecone is bumpy. Texture is a property you discover by using your sense of touch.

sections.heading: Weight and Other Properties
body: Weight tells you how heavy or light something is. A feather is very light, while a bowling ball is very heavy. Other useful properties include whether something is shiny or dull, hard or soft, and whether it bends or breaks. All these clues help you describe matter!

sections.heading: Properties Review
body: Properties like color, size, shape, texture, and weight help us describe and compare objects. Scientists use properties to sort and study different types of matter. The more properties you notice, the better you can describe the world around you!

question.text: What property describes how something feels when you touch it?

lessons.title: Heating and Cooling
lessons.description: See what happens when you heat or cool matter.

sections.heading: What You'll Learn
body: In this lesson, you will see what happens when you heat or cool different materials. Temperature changes can make matter melt, freeze, or even boil! By the end, you'll understand how heating and cooling can completely change the way matter looks and behaves.

sections.heading: Melting — Solid to Liquid
body: When you heat a solid, it can melt and become a liquid. Think about an ice cream cone on a hot day — the ice cream melts and drips down your hand! Butter melts in a hot pan, and chocolate melts in your mouth. Melting happens when a solid gets warm enough.

sections.heading: Boiling — Liquid to Gas
body: If you keep heating a liquid, it will eventually boil and turn into a gas. When water boils in a pot, you can see bubbles rising and steam floating up into the air. That steam is water that has turned into a gas called water vapor.

sections.heading: Freezing — Liquid to Solid
body: When you cool a liquid enough, it freezes and becomes a solid. Water turns into ice when it gets very cold. You can see this when you put a tray of water in the freezer and it turns into ice cubes. Freezing is the opposite of melting!

sections.heading: Reversible Changes
body: Many heating and cooling changes can be reversed. You can melt an ice cube into water, then freeze the water back into ice. You can melt chocolate, then let it cool and harden again. These are called reversible changes because you can go back and forth.

sections.heading: Heating and Cooling Review
body: Heating makes solids melt into liquids and liquids boil into gases. Cooling makes gases condense into liquids and liquids freeze into solids. Many of these changes are reversible, which means they can happen again and again!

question.text: What is it called when a liquid gets cold enough to become a solid?

lessons.title: Mixing Materials
lessons.description: Explore what happens when you mix things together.

sections.heading: What You'll Learn
body: In this lesson, you will explore what happens when you mix different materials together. Some mixtures can be separated easily, while others create something completely new. By the end, you'll understand the difference and be able to spot mixtures all around you!

sections.heading: What Is a Mixture?
body: A mixture is what you get when you combine two or more materials together. In many mixtures, the materials don't actually change — they just sit next to each other. A bowl of trail mix is a mixture because you can still pick out the nuts, raisins, and chocolate pieces.

sections.heading: Ways to Separate Mixtures
body: You can separate many mixtures using simple methods. A strainer or sieve can separate pasta from water. A magnet can pull metal paper clips out of a pile of sand. Filtering, sieving, and picking things apart are all ways to undo a mixture.

sections.heading: Dissolving
body: Some materials dissolve when you mix them with a liquid. When you stir sugar into water, the sugar seems to disappear — but it's still there! The water tastes sweet because the tiny sugar particles have spread out evenly in the water. This is called a solution.

sections.heading: Mixtures That Make Something New
body: Sometimes mixing materials creates something totally new that can't easily be separated. When you mix baking soda and vinegar, they fizz and bubble, creating a gas. Baking a cake mixes flour, eggs, and sugar into something you can't unmix. These are called irreversible changes.

sections.heading: Mixing Materials Review
body: Mixtures combine two or more materials. Some mixtures can be separated easily using tools like strainers or magnets. Other mixtures, like dissolving sugar in water or mixing baking soda with vinegar, are harder or impossible to undo. Science is all about exploring what happens when things come together!

question.text: What happens when you stir sugar into water?
